newsitem.title: UK: WEEK AHEAD - G7, Tankan and supply the focus.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - G7, Tankan and supply the focus.

text.p: Japanese issues will draw most attention in financial markets this week as they digest news from the weekend summit of G7 leaders and Japan's Tankan survey of corporate sentiment, analysts said.
Debt supply on both sides of the Atlantic will also feature.

Leaders of the Group of Seven nations ended their summit in Denver, Colorado, on Sunday, giving Russia new clout in their club and celebrating a sound global economy but otherwise breaking little new ground.

Unlike many previous summits, the meeting was not hijacked by an economic or political crisis. But the final communique expressed concern over Japanese trade surpluses and the high unemployment in continental Europe and said the United States must prevent its booming economy spinning into inflation.

Apart from analysing the Denver meeting, markets will scrutinise the Bank of Japan's second-quarter Tankan survey of corporate sentiment on Wednesday for indications of firm growth in the Japanese economy.

"Any signs that sentiment is recovering sharply will bring forward expectations of a rate move by the Bank of Japan," Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ International in London, said. He said IBJ was anticipating a fairly soft report.

Analysts said few significant U.S. economic data were due, but supply would be prominent. The U.S. Treasury will auction $15.5 billion of two-year notes on Tuesday and $11.5 billion of five-year paper on Wednesday.

"They will be a focus," said Eric Fishwick, international economist at Nikko Europe in London. "The short end of the U.S. curve is pretty aggressively pricing in flat rates. So in that sort of environment auctions at the short end are important."
Fishwick said May durable goods orders on Wednesday would be the U.S. indicator getting most attention.
David Smith, chief economist at Williams de Broe in London, said the final revision to first quarter real GDP might also promote some reaction.

While the economic background now seemed to indicate the Federal Market Open Committee will likely hold rates when it meets on July 1-2, Smith said any unexpectedly strong figures might cause people to change their views.

In Europe too supply will be a focus. The British Treasury will auction the 7.25 percent gilt due 2007 on Wednesday. Edmonds said the schedule for Germany's third quarter auction might be released. But few European data were to be published.
Fishwick said European markets would continue to be dominated by speculation about progress on European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

"Further close scrutiny will be given to any comments from the new French administration and in Germany to both the Bundesbank and the government as to how the battle between EMU hard-liners and the politicians in Germany works out," he said.
Smith said the European political backdrop provided more of a focus than the economic situation. "There is still general uncertainty as to which way (French Prime Minister) Jospin will jump," he said
